newsitem.title: UK: Mars meteorite inspires search for life in space.
newsitem.headline: Mars meteorite inspires search for life in space.

text.p: Astronomers looking for signs of extra-terrestrial life were revitalised when U.S. scientists said they had found evidence of life on Mars.

NASA's claim that tiny holes in a 16-million-year-old meteorite were the fossilised remains of bacteria was controversial at best. But it fired the imagination of the world and gave new impetus to the flagging U.S. space programme.
British scientists have now backed up NASA, saying that they had found additional evidence that an ancient chunk of Mars rock had once harboured bacteria.
They also said closer examination of a second meteorite turned up chemical traces that might have been left by ancient micro-organisms.
"We think that this is backing for the supposition that there is life on Mars," Colin Pillinger, an astronomer at Britain's Open University, told a news conference on Thursday.
Pillinger and colleagues gathered a variety of experts who said they had found compelling body of evidence suggesting that there really was "life out there."
Biologists such as Don Cowan of University College, London, told about extremophiles -- bacteria that can live in hotter-than-boiling water or deep inside the earth where there is no air.
If life can exist in such hostile environments on Earth, perhaps it can also survive on inhospitable planets, he said.

David DesMarais of NASA's Ames Research Centre said scientists would meet there later this month to discuss looking for life in sub-surface oceans on Jupiter's moon Europa. Such a mission could be launched soon after 2005, he said.
Scientists at London's Natural History Museum said they would release for examination a meteorite they had been saving since 1913. The meteorite, which fell on Egypt in 1911, is virtually untouched.

"We think the time is nigh," said Monica Grady, the museum's expert on meteorites. She said one piece of the meteorite would still contain pristine Martian atmospheric gases which could give hints about conditions on the planet in years past.
What scientists really need from Mars now is a piece of sedimentary rock -- one that formed at the bottom of an ocean or a river. Such rocks contain the best fossils of ancient life on Earth.

But Pillinger said: "We don't have any sedimentary rocks from Mars. We have to work with what we have." That meant working with meteorites, at least until a Mars mission could bring back more samples from the red planet.
Asked what would form definitive proof of extra-terrestial life, Pillinger, only half-jokingly, said: "Something that wiggled, I suppose."
Nonetheless, astronomers agree that the evidence from the Mars meteorites had given them fresh hope.

"It's changed my life, let me tell you," said Alan Penny of the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory in Didcot, central England. "In 15 years' time we should know whether there are planets with life on them near us."
Penny said NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA) were working on a new telescope that, once deployed near Jupiter, would scan nearby stars for planets that resemble Earth.
It would be able to see even better than the Hubble Space Telescope now orbiting Earth. Measurements could show whether there was water on the planets and possibly even life.
"It could be (just) plankton," Penny said. "But of course if you found it you would build a bigger telescope and in 100 years you could build a starship and go there."
